title.en: Solubility and concentration of a solution
A spoon of sugar in hot and cold tea

text.en: Stir one spoon of sugar into cold tea and some stays at the bottom, but in hot tea it vanishes at once. There is a limit to how much a solvent can dissolve, and chemists measure that limit as solubility.

Solubility is the number of grams of a solute that can dissolve in 100 g of a solvent to form a saturated solution at a given temperature and pressure.
For example, 36 g of sodium chloride dissolves in 100 g of water at 25 degree C, so the solubility of NaCl in water is 36 g at that temperature.
Mathematically, solubility = mass of solute divided by mass of solvent, multiplied by 100.
The nature of solute and solvent matters: like dissolves like, so polar common salt dissolves in polar water, and non-polar fat dissolves in non-polar ether.
Temperature matters too: the solubility of a solid in a liquid generally increases with temperature, so more sugar dissolves in warm water than in cold water.
A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature, an unsaturated solution holds less solute than the saturated one, and a supersaturated solution holds more, so it is unstable and crystals appear when it is disturbed.
Dilute and concentrated are relative terms: of two solutions with the same solute and solvent, the one with more solute per amount of solvent is concentrated.
Concentration is the amount of solute present in a given amount of solution, and the textbook uses percentage by mass and percentage by volume.
Mass percentage = mass of solute divided by mass of solution, multiplied by 100; it is used when the solute is a solid and the solvent a liquid, and for ointments it is written w/w.
Volume percentage, v/v = volume of solute divided by volume of solution, multiplied by 100; it is used when both are liquids, as in mouth wash and antiseptics, and it falls when temperature rises because liquids expand.
Remember that the mass of the solution is the mass of solute plus the mass of solvent, so 10 g of sugar in 90 g of water makes a 10 percent solution, not 11 percent.

problem.en: 1.5 g of a solute dissolves in 15 g of water to give a saturated solution at 298 K. Find the solubility. Then find the mass percentage of a solution of 20 g sugar in 180 g water.

text.en: Solubility = mass of solute / mass of solvent x 100 = 1.5 / 15 x 100.

why.en: Solubility is always per 100 g of solvent.

text.en: = 10 g per 100 g of water at 298 K.

why.en: Do the division first, then multiply by 100.

text.en: For the sugar solution, mass of solution = 20 + 180 = 200 g.

why.en: Add solute and solvent to get the solution.
Divide by the solution, not by the solvent.

prompt.en: Explain solubility, the three kinds of solutions by amount of solute, and how mass percentage is calculated.

requiredIdeas.en: Solubility is grams per 100 g solvent
Mass percent uses the mass of the whole solution

commonMisconceptions.en: Dividing by the mass of solvent instead of the solution for percentage
Thinking dilute means unsaturated and concentrated means saturated

points.en: Solubility = mass of solute / mass of solvent x 100, at a given temperature.
Saturated, unsaturated and supersaturated solutions differ in the amount of solute held.
Mass percentage = mass of solute / mass of solution x 100.
Volume percentage is used for liquid in liquid solutions.
